root_cause.text: KVM’s SEV/SEV-ES VMSA sync path (`sev_es_sync_vmsa()` in `arch/x86/kvm/svm/sev.c`) did not check whether the vCPU had already been launched and its VMSA encrypted, so it could try to write to guest-private memory after launch, triggering an RMP violation on SNP hosts.
root_cause.evidence: The patch adds `if (vcpu->arch.guest_state_protected) return -EINVAL;` at the start of `sev_es_sync_vmsa()`, and the CVE says the bug occurs when “synchronizing vCPU state to its associated VMSA if the vCPU has already been launched, i.e. if the VMSA has already been encrypted,” causing “accessing guest-private memory” to generate an “RMP #PF” and panic the host.

intent_record.intent_summary: Reject VMSA synchronization when guest state is already protected to prevent invalid SEV-ES handling.
intent_record.what: In `sev_es_sync_vmsa(struct vcpu_svm *svm)`, a new early return was added: if `vcpu->arch.guest_state_protected` is true, the function now returns `-EINVAL` before performing the existing debug-field validation and VMSA encryption work.
intent_record.how: At runtime, the function now rejects attempts to sync the VMSA when the guest state is already marked protected, preventing this code path from operating on an incompatible protected guest state and avoiding invalid VMSA synchronization.

grouping_result.intent: Reject VMSA synchronization when guest state is already protected to prevent invalid SEV-ES handling.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it rejects VMSA synchronization once guest state is already protected/launched, preventing writes to private guest memory after encryption and avoiding the RMP violation.

candidates.rationale: This is the only pre-fix guard shown in the VMSA sync path, and it checks debug state rather than whether the vCPU has already been launched/protected. The missing launch/protected-state check allowed the code to proceed into VMSA writes after launch, which can trigger an RMP violation on SNP hosts.

vuln_statements.explanation: This is the only guard in sev_es_sync_vmsa() before VMSA writes, but it checks guest debug/DR7 state rather than whether the vCPU has already been launched and its VMSA encrypted. Because the missing launch/protected-state check allowed the function to continue into guest-private memory writes after launch, it could trigger an RMP violation on SNP hosts.

bic_trace_step.reason: The shown function is `sev_es_sync_vmsa()` and it only copies/synchronizes the VMSA state: `struct sev_es_save_area *save = svm->sev_es.vmsa;`, checks debug fields, then does `memcpy(save, &svm->vmcb->save, sizeof(svm->vmcb->save));` and updates registers. The vulnerable root cause described is a missing check for whether the vCPU had already been launched/encrypted before writing to guest-private memory, but there is no launch-state guard here (no check like launched/encrypted/RMP-safe state) and no logic related to avoiding writes after launch. The code is instead about using a separate SEV-ES save area, so the specific vulnerable construct is absent in this snippet.
